Haile Selassie. The emperor of Ethiopia from 1930 until his overthrow in 1974, and the last ruling member of Ethiopia's Solomonic dynasty. He was a modernizer and pan-Africanist who championed African sovereignty and dignity, becoming a spiritual icon in Rastafarianism while defending his nation against Italian fascism and colonialism.

He was crowned emperor in 1930, taking the throne name Haile Selassie, meaning "Might of the Trinity," after decades of modernizing Ethiopian government and military as regent and then heir. When Italy invaded in 1935, he defended Ethiopia's independence and sovereignty, appealing to the League of Nations in a dramatic speech that galvanized anti-colonial sentiment worldwide. During the Italian occupation from 1936 to 1941, he fled Ethiopia and lived in exile in Britain. After British-led forces liberated the country, he returned and rebuilt the nation into a respected regional power.

In 1963, he founded the Organisation of African Unity in Addis Ababa, positioning Ethiopia as the symbolic capital and himself as a continental leader. He became a divinity figure in Rastafarianism, with Jamaican and Caribbean followers revering him as the incarnation of God, though he was Coptic Christian and never embraced the faith. In 1974, he was overthrown in a Marxist military coup and died in captivity the following year, ending the Solomonic dynasty's three-thousand-year reign. He connects to other pan-Africanists like Kwame Nkrumah, who competed for continental leadership, and to Nelson Mandela, another African icon of a later generation.
